x6-tools-techniques-index.title: Appendix X6: tools and techniques grouped by purpose (132 tools; group counts) and index
x6-tools-techniques-index.notes: Sixth Edition groups tools and techniques by intent - the group names the intent and the members are alternative methods (e.g., data gathering includes brainstorming, interviews, market research) - reflecting the emphasis on tailoring. 132 individual tools and techniques, representing good practice on most projects most of the time. Groups and counts: data gathering 9; data analysis 27; data representation 15; decision-making 2; communication skills 2; interpersonal and team skills 17; ungrouped 60. Table X6-1 indexes each tool by group and the processes using it, with the describing process in bold (bolding not preserved in extraction). Rows read across PDF 723-731: data gathering (benchmarking, brainstorming, check sheets, checklists, focus groups, interviews, market research, questionnaires and surveys, statistical sampling); data analysis (alternatives analysis, assessment of other risk parameters, assumption and constraint analysis, cost of quality, cost-benefit analysis, decision tree analysis, document analysis, earned value analysis, influence diagrams, iteration burndown chart, make-or-buy analysis, performance reviews, process analysis, proposal evaluation, regression analysis, reserve analysis, risk data quality assessment, risk probability and impact assessment, root cause analysis, sensitivity analysis, simulation, stakeholder analysis, SWOT analysis, technical performance analysis, trend analysis, variance analysis, what-if scenario analysis); data representation (affinity diagrams, cause-and-effect diagrams, control charts, flowcharts, hierarchical charts, histograms, logical data model, matrix diagrams, matrix-based charts, mind mapping, probability and impact matrix, scatter diagrams, stakeholder engagement assessment matrix, stakeholder mapping/representation, text-oriented formats); decision-making (multicriteria decision analysis, voting); communication skills (feedback, presentations); interpersonal and team skills (active listening, communication styles assessment, conflict management, cultural awareness, decision making, emotional intelligence, facilitation, influencing, leadership, meeting management, motivation, negotiation, networking, nominal group technique, observation/conversation, political awareness, team building); ungrouped (advertising, agile release planning, analogous estimating, audits, bidder conferences, bottom-up estimating, change control tools, claims administration, colocation, communication methods, communication models, communication requirements analysis, communication technology, context diagram, contingent response strategies, cost aggregation, critical path method, decomposition, dependency determination and integration, Design for X, expert judgment, financing, funding limit reconciliation, ground rules, historical information review, individual and team assessments, information management, inspections, knowledge management, leads and lags, meetings, organizational theory, parametric estimating, pre-assignment, precedence diagramming method, problem solving, product analysis, PMIS, project reporting, prompt lists, prototypes, quality improvement methods, recognition and rewards, representations of uncertainty, resource optimization, risk categorization, rolling wave planning, schedule compression, schedule network analysis, source selection analysis, strategies for opportunities/overall risk/threats, test and inspection planning, testing/product evaluations, three-point estimating, to-complete performance index, training, virtual teams). Source notes: several index cells do not match the per-process figures (e.g., alternatives analysis against 5.4 instead of 5.3; decomposition against 6.3 instead of 6.2; 'matrix-based charts' appears for 9.1 where the process text says responsibility assignment matrix; project reporting listed against 8.2 though it is a 10.2 tool) - lessons and questions take tool-to-process mappings from the per-process ITTO figures (ittos.json and topic notes) and use X6 only for the grouping concept, names and counts.

g-glossary-scope-acronyms.title: Glossary: inclusion/exclusion rules and common acronyms
g-glossary-scope-acronyms.notes: Includes terms unique or nearly unique to project management (project scope statement, work package, WBS, CPM) and terms used differently or more narrowly than in everyday usage (early start date); excludes application-area-specific terms, terms used as in everyday language (calendar day, delay), compound terms clear from their parts, obvious variants, and terms used once and not critical. Acronyms: AC, BAC, CCB, COQ, CPAF, CPFF, CPI, CPIF, CPM, CV, EAC, EF, ES, ETC, EV, EVM, FF (finish-to-finish), FFP, FPEPA, FPIF, FS, IFB (invitation for bid - appears in the acronym list though not discussed in the body), LF, LOE (level of effort), LS, OBS, PDM, PMBOK, PV, QFD, RACI, RAM, RBS (in the acronym list RBS = risk breakdown structure; the body also uses 'resource breakdown structure' without an acronym - lessons spell both out), RFI, RFP, RFQ, SF, SOW, SPI, SS, SV, SWOT, T&M, WBS, VAC.

g-glossary-a-c.title: Glossary definitions A-C (Acceptance Criteria to Criteria): key precise wordings and glossary-only facts
g-glossary-a-c.notes: Definitions are consistent with the body; items noted for teaching precision: accuracy (within a quality management system, an assessment of correctness); acquisition (obtaining human and material resources; implies a cost, not necessarily financial); activity (a distinct, scheduled portion of work); activity duration (calendar time between start and finish); actual duration (actual start to the data date if in progress, or to actual finish); adaptive life cycle (a project life cycle that is iterative or incremental); agreements (any document or communication defining initial intentions - contract, MOU, letters of agreement, verbal agreements, email); assumption (a factor considered true, real or certain without proof or demonstration); attribute sampling (noting presence or absence of a characteristic in each unit); authority (the right to apply resources, expend funds, make decisions or give approvals); backward pass (calculating late start and late finish dates working backward from the project end date); baseline (approved version of a work product changed only through formal change control, used for comparison); benefits management plan (processes for creating, maximising and sustaining benefits of a project or program); bid documents (all documents used to solicit information, quotations or proposals); budget (approved estimate for the project, any WBS component or activity); buffer (see reserve); cause and effect diagram (a decomposition technique tracing an undesirable effect back to its root cause); change (modification to any formally controlled deliverable, plan component or document); change control system (procedures describing how modifications to deliverables and documentation are managed); change log (comprehensive list of submitted changes and their status); change management plan (establishes the CCB, documents its authority, describes how the change control system is implemented); checklist analysis; checksheets (tally sheet usable as a checklist when gathering data); claim (request, demand or assertion of rights by a seller against a buyer or vice versa under a contract, e.g., for a disputed change); claims administration; code of accounts (numbering system uniquely identifying each WBS component); colocation (team physically close to improve communication, relationships and productivity); communication requirements analysis (via interviews, workshops, lessons learned); configuration management plan and system; conformance (results within limits defining acceptable variation); constraint (limiting factor affecting execution of a project, program, portfolio or process); contingency (an event that could affect execution and may be accounted for with a reserve); contingency reserve (time or money in the schedule or cost baseline for known risks with active response strategies); contract (mutually binding agreement obligating the seller to provide and the buyer to pay); contract change control system; control (compare actual with planned, analyse variances, assess trends, evaluate alternatives, recommend corrective action); control account (management control point integrating scope, budget, actual cost and schedule and comparing to EV); control chart (process data over time against control limits with a centreline to detect trends); control limits - glossary-only detail: the area of three standard deviations either side of the centreline or mean of a normal distribution, reflecting expected variation (see also specification limits); cost baseline (excludes management reserves); cost-benefit analysis (benefits against costs); CPAF/CPFF/CPIF and cost-reimbursable contract definitions consistent with Section 12; crashing; criteria. The CCB definition here says 'approving, delaying, or rejecting' where the body says 'deferring' - same meaning.
